Catalogue reference: ZPER 34/59 p345 From the Black Death to COVID-19, The National Archives holds numerous collections that shed light on official responses to pandemics, epidemics, infection and disease. Authors Paul Carter Roles Author Researcher Principal Records Specialist for Collaborative Projects Dr Natasha Kitcher Roles Author Researcher Digital Researcher Dr Laura Robson-Mainwaring Roles Author Researcher Principal Records Specialist – Modern Health Dr Euan Roger Roles Author Researcher Principal Records Specialist (Medieval) Dr Giorgia Tolfo Roles Author Researcher Collections Researcher On this page Medical and welfare history at The National Archives Responses to plague Smallpox in the late 18th and 19th centuries The 1918–1919 influenza pandemic The HIV pandemic (1981 to early 1990s) COVID-19 (2020–2023) Medical and welfare history at The National Archives From rules and orders that respond to outbreaks of plague and cholera, to more recent HIV and COVID-19 health campaigns, our records document changing attitudes and responses towards diseases. Collections at The National Archives reveal the increasing involvement of the state in regulating and coordinating health prevention and emergency medical schemes. What follows is a short journey through four key moments in time, when the state had to respond to the spread of epidemics and diseases. Responses to plague When we think of plague in England, two major epidemics might come to mind: the Black Death of 1348–1349 and the Great Plague of 1665–1666. These two outbreaks occurred during the centuries-long second plague pandemic caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. Records held in our collections shed light on the impromptu responses to outbreaks, such as a letter directed from Edward III to the sheriffs of London in 1349, ordering them to clean the streets of faeces and filth which were causing disease to spread. From 1517, England introduced quarantine for the first time, prompted by Henry VIII’s personal fears about the spread of disease. The earliest state‑led measures were enforced at Windsor Castle. Anyone leaving to obtain food, drink, or other necessities had to carry a white staff to signal distance, and a pole fixed to the house warned others of infection. These restrictions remained in place for forty days after the last sign of illness. These longer-term measures were soon copied in London and Oxford in 1518. In Oxford, however, the implementation of quarantine regulations was controversial. It became the subject of debate among the King’s Council (a group of the king's advisers). In particularly the Council reviewed whether the annual Austin Friars’ fair (due to take place a fortnight later) should continue as normal. Concerns about an influx into Oxford of infected persons from London were balanced against open hostility from certain merchants, who felt the rules limited their trading activity. Ultimately, the fair was allowed to go ahead as planned. Toggle partial transcript The king’s grace commanded his council here to debate this matter among themselves, whether it should be best that the fair in the Austin Friars in Oxford, which after the old custom shall be now within14 days, should be stopped or not, for it is thought that for the resort of people as well from London as from other infect places [w]hether Oxford shall be in as evil case by the beginning of the next term as London. Also, it was said in the said council that in stopping and letting of the said fair there should ensue grogs and murmurs among the king’s subjects, specially in London, when they would think that men went about utterly to destroy them, if with other their misfortunes they should also be kept from their fairs and markets. Letter among the State Papers discussing concerns around rules to restrict infection, including whether fairs and markets in Oxford should be cancelled or allowed to proceed, 1518. Catalogue reference: SP 1/16, f. 244 Over the course of the 16th and into the 17th centuries, regulations became stricter, and were often controversial, but the idea of quarantine would persist as one tool in the state’s responses to infectious disease. Toggle partial transcript You are to take care, that no stranger be permitted to lodge or abide in any city, town, or village without a sufficient certificate of health and the consent of the next Justice of Peace or Chief Magistrate… That no household goods whatsoever be received into any city, borough, town, village or hamlet, coming from any place suspected to be infected with the plague, without sufficient certificate. That all public meetings and concourses of people, as much as may be (especially to funerals, wakes, or revels) be prohibited where there is any suspicion of the plague That no vagabonds nor beggars be permitted to go and wander about the country, or in any other city or place, and that you appoint watching and warding to that end, and that all public places (especially streets and passages) be kept sweet and clean, and that all laystalls, dunghills, and slaughter houses near any dwellings be removed to places more remote. That order be given to all householders to keep their dwelling houses sweet and clean, and to keep shut all windows opening towards infected houses. Rules and Orders for preventing the spread of the plague in 1666. Catalogue reference: SP 29/155, ff. 142-3 In pictures Plague Efforts to guard against the spread of historic pandemics can be found in the records of our collection, from individuals and the state. Smallpox in the late 18th and 19th centuries The state’s response to smallpox in the late 18th and 19th centuries combined emerging scientific knowledge with administrative innovation. Smallpox was one of the most lethal diseases of the period, killing an average of around 3,000 people per million annually in England between 1700 and 1797. The first significant medical intervention was variolation, an early form of inoculation, introduced to the UK in the early 18th century. This involved inserting matter from a smallpox pustule into the skin of an uninfected person. Though risky, inoculation sharply reduced mortality compared to natural infection and was seen as a statistical breakthrough. Its early use was experimental and controversial. Six prisoners at Newgate were offered reduced sentences in return for undergoing the procedure, all of whom survived. Nevertheless, inoculation remained expensive and inaccessible to the poor, limiting its wider impact. As a result, smallpox continued to be a major killer throughout the 18th century. A decisive breakthrough came in the late 1790s with British physician Edward Jenner’s development of vaccination, using cowpox virus. This was a global scientific first. Parishes increasingly adopted vaccination programmes, contracting doctors to vaccinate the poor and funding this through the rates raised by the Elizabethan poor law (Poor Law Act, 1601). For the poorest sections of society, this marked a major advance in public health provision. The founding of the National Vaccine Establishment in 1808 further promoted widespread uptake. 'An Acte for the Releife of the Poore', 1601. This act, popularly known as the Elizabethan Poor Law, formalized poor relief distribution in England and Wales. Catalogue reference: YHL/PO/PU/1/1601/43Eliz1n2 Vaccination return under the Vaccination Extension Act for Llanfyllin, Monmouthshire, for the year ended 29 September 1849. Shows the names of vaccinators and the number of people vaccinated, 21 January 1850. Catalogue reference: MH 12/16545/267 Following the creation of the centralised New Poor Law in 1834, vaccination became fully integrated into the state welfare system. A series of parliamentary acts made vaccination compulsory and free, while banning inoculation altogether. Boards of Poor Law Guardians employed vaccinators, often their own medical officers, to vaccinate local populations at a set cost per head. Vaccination cases were formally reported and recorded, creating a growing body of administrative and medical data. Toggle transcript RICHMOND UNION. COMPULSORY VACCINATION. It is requested that Parents of Children and all other Persons will Take Notice of the provisions made by the several Acts of the 3rd & 4th and 16th & 17th years of the reign of Queen Victoria, for the Extension of Vaccination with the Cow Pox, and the Prevention of the Spread of Small Pox; and to Make Compulsory the Practice of Vaccination upon the Parents and Guardians of Children. Richmond Union smallpox vaccination poster, 1856. Catalogue reference: MH 12/12599 The effectiveness of vaccination lay in the combination of scientific observation, repeatedly measurable health outcomes, and the administrative machinery provided by central law making and local government units (Poor Law Unions). Between 1857 to 1866, at a time of compulsory vaccination, average smallpox deaths per million per year fell to 214. Nevertheless, an anti-vaccination movement was active in the late-Victorian period, setting up a mirror image of the British experience of COVID-19 in the 2020s. Toggle transcript REPTILE THIS IS TO give you warning THAT IF YOU DO NOT give up your ABOMINABLE OFFICE you will not Live To see next Summer: you mean skulking venomous TOAD you WILL wade through THE BLOOD OF innocient CHILDREN FOR THE SAKE OF A FEW pounds i hope THAT EVERY pound you get WILL SINK you a THOUSAND Miles FARTHER INTO HELL And Heat it TEN Thousand Times hotter Extract from an anonymous anti-vaccination letter sent to John Gott, Vaccination Officer, Keighley Poor Law Union in late 1882. Catalogue reference: MH 12/15177 The 1918–1919 influenza pandemic The 1918–1919 influenza pandemic was among the deadliest disease outbreaks in modern history, killing an estimated 50 million people, far more than the First World War. Around 250,000 people in Britain died, with every part of society affected. Wartime overcrowding and poor sanitation in military camps and trenches contributed to the virus’s spread. Early signs of the outbreak appear in government records, such as a May 1918 Cabinet Office report noting over 200 influenza cases aboard H.M.S. Weymouth. Much of the early scientific work on the virus was conducted by the Army Pathology Advisory Committee, which collaborated closely with the Medical Research Committee. Medical Research Committee pamphlet, Studies of Influenza in Hospitals of the British Armies in France, 1918 (1919). Catalogue reference: FD 4/36 At the time, national health responsibilities sat with the Local Government Board, but most practical measures were carried out by local authorities. During the severe second wave of influenza in autumn 1918, Medical Officers of Health introduced a number of measures. They restricted entry to theatres, cinemas, and dance halls, isolated the sick, and issued advice through newspapers urging people to stay home when feverish and ventilate rooms. Schools often closed briefly, though no national directive was issued. The unknowns surrounding the flu meant that there was a lack of agreement in the medical community about how best to treat it. Doctors were only able to treat its symptoms. This led to a reliance on commercial remedies for prevention and treatment such as Condy’s Fluid (a sore throat treatment using permanganate potassium), throat lozenges, medicated wines, carbolic vaporizers (a device to kill airborne bacteria), and portable Turkish (vapour) baths. Example of an influenza vapour bath, dating from 1848. Catalogue reference: BT 45/7/1396 In early 1919, as a third wave appeared, medical practitioners had to report any cases of primary pneumonia and acute influenza pneumonia, amid fears that soldiers returning home from the war would worsen the outbreak. Public information efforts continued. Arthur Newsholme, Chief Medical Officer of the Local Government Board, commissioned the silent film Dr. Wise on Influenza. The film promoted ventilation, rest, and hygiene measures such as gargling and nasal douching. youtube.com Watch Dr. Wise on Influenza (1919) Public information film on the Influenza pandemic (18 minutes, 10 seconds). The pandemic highlighted weaknesses in Britain’s health administration and contributed to the creation of the Ministry of Health in November 1919 . This reform was widely supported in the press as public interest in health surged after the crisis. Healthcare in the 1920s continued to be shaped by a society still recovering from the First World War and the deadly influenza pandemic. In pictures Health in the 1920s The ever-shifting role of the state in public health is revealed in our records from the 1920s, drawn from material from across government departments. The HIV pandemic (1981 to early 1990s) HIV emerged globally in the early 1980s and reached the United Kingdom by 1981–82. By the mid‑1980s, rising case numbers and growing public concern prompted the government to act, investing in medical research and measures to limit transmission. In 1986, it launched the nationwide ‘Don’t Die of Ignorance’ public health campaign. This was designed to make people aware of the risks of HIV, quickly deliver clear, accessible information on how it is spread, how to reduce risk, and how to respond to possible exposure. Although mass‑media health messaging had precedents, nothing matched the scale, visual impact, and international resonance of this campaign. Records about the commissioning of the campaign expose internal tensions, political sensitivities, and the challenges of crafting effective messaging during a period of scientific uncertainty and public anxiety. Among these is a 1986 memo from David Willetts, of the Policy Unit, urging swift action. Margaret Thatcher’s handwritten annotation, 'Do we have to have the section on risky sex? I should have thought it could do immense harm if young teenagers were to read it', illustrates political discomfort around sexual content, and the broader clash between public health necessity and social conservatism. Toggle partial transcript Norman Fowler is proposing to place explicit and distasteful advertisements about AIDS in all the Sunday papers. The AIDS problem is now so serious that we must do as he proposes, though his advert could open with more facts about the spread of AIDS. We have so far had 275 cases of clinical AIDS in this country. But approximately 20,000 people are known to be carrying the virus. The Chief Medical Officer estimates that perhaps 25% of these people go on to develop clinical AIDS. But he may be optimistic - it is possible that they will all develop AIDS over the coming years. The cost of treating someone with clinical AIDS is very cautiously estimated at £10,000-£20,000. That represents a bill between £50m and £100m just for the people currently with the virus who can be expected to catch the disease. The number of people with the virus is doubling every year. The virus is mainly transmitted between homosexuals and between drug addicts who share contaminated needles. In Edinburgh 50% of drug addicts have the virus (as against 10% of addicts elsewhere) because pharmacists clamped down on providing needles for addicts. The challenge is to achieve proper public health supervision of addicts without encouraging drug-taking. AIDS isn't just transmitted between drug-takers and homosexuals. It can also be transmitted by normal intercourse. The following causal chain is perfectly possible: a drug-taker who finances her addiction by prostitution transmits the virus to a male client who passes it on to his wife who gives birth to a baby with the virus. These are the sorts of mechanism whereby AIDS can spread out to the population at large. David Willetts Letter by David Willetts to Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher on the urgency of an AIDS public health campaign. Catalogue reference: PREM 19/1863 Storyboards for the ’ Monolith’ television and cinema advert (shown below), unused newspaper designs, and proofs of the household leaflet demonstrate how campaign designers navigated limited scientific knowledge, public fear, and stigma. The prominence of stark imagery and frank language signalled a new, fear‑based marketing strategy. This marked a turning point in late‑20th‑century public health communication, highlighting the growing power of mass media to shape national understanding and influence behaviour during a public health emergency. Toggle partial transcript AIDS. Monolith. 40 secs. There is a disease today that is potentially more deadly... ...than the deadliest bomb. This virus can be passed during sexual intercourse, so anyone can get it male or female, gay or straight. The numbers who are already infected are rising, be very careful who you have sex with. Protect yourself, and use a condom, and read this leaflet when it arrives. Today AIDS is the fact of life you cannot ignore ignore it and it could be the death of you. Storyboard for the AIDS ‘Monolith’ advert, 1986. Catalogue reference: JA 235/57 In pictures HIV and AIDS We hold an extensive range of material related to the HIV and AIDS epidemic of the 1980 and 1990s. Explore them here. COVID-19 (2020–2023) The outbreak of COVID-19 was the most documented pandemic in history, owing to it being one of the first global pandemics since the invention of the world wide web in 1989. The first cases of coronavirus were reported in 2019, and the virus was first found in the UK on 31 January 2020. By 16 March 2020 the Prime Minister began daily briefings, with a nationwide lockdown announced the following week, on 23 March. Archived page Prime Minister Boris Johnson’s speech announcing lockdown Boris Johnson gives an important update on COVID-19. During the COVID‑19 pandemic, the UK Government Web Archive (UKGWA) team, responsible for capturing and preserving online government information, archived at least 71.5 million more web documents than usual. They created an extensive record of how the crisis unfolded and how official advice rapidly evolved. On the UKGWA site, timeline pages make it possible to track how any specific URL changed over time. The COVID-19 dashboard and the NHS COVID-19 page are two particularly valuable examples for understanding the progression of COVID‑19. These pages allow users to follow the spread of the virus and the growing complexity of the government’s digital response. The earliest version of the COVID-19 dashboard from 14 April 2020 was extremely simple, displaying only one graph and a few key figures. By late 2020 it featured an interactive map and by mid‑2021 it included data on infections, hospitalisations and vaccination. GOV.UK Coronavirus dashboard showing data as of 14 April 2020. GOV.UK Coronavirus dashboard showing data archived on 6 March 2024. Archived page Timeline of the Government COVID-19 dashboard UK Government Web Archive of the COVID-19 dashboard. The NHS website reveals how advice related to COVID-19 changed throughout the pandemic. The page was first created in February 2020 when the risk to individuals was reported to be low. The first NHS COVID-19 webpage, archived on 13 February 2020. You can follow the progress of the pandemic across these sites up until 2023, with the ongoing COVID-19 Inquiry website also forming part of the collection. To see the most recent capture of the Inquiry website and how it has progressed over the years, view the Inquiry timeline. The National Archives' collections shed light on official responses to public health emergencies across the centuries. This research reveals the increasing involvement of the state in health education, disease prevention and data capture. Archived page COVID-19 Public Inquiry Archive Timeline UK Government Web Archive for the COVID-19 Public Inquiry. Menu Visit What’s on Explore the collection Help using the archive Education Professional guidance and services Search Shop Home Explore the collection Stories from the collection Record revealed Freddie Mercury’s naturalisation certificate Freddie Mercury was naturalised as a British citizen in 1969. This record tells the story of how he emigrated from Zanzibar to the UK and became a rock music icon. Images Image 1 of 3 Freddie Mercury naturalisation certificate page one, 1969. Catalogue reference: HO 334/1421/117889 Transcript HO 334/1421/117889 117889 Home Office Form R1 (Second Copy) B. 211808 British Nationality Act 1948, Section 6 (1) Commonwealth Immigrants Act 1962, Section 12 (2) Application for registration as a citizen of the United Kingdom and colonies made by a British Subject or Citizen of the Republic of Ireland on the ground of ordinary residence or crown service Caution: to give false information on this form purposely or recklessly is a criminal offence punishable with imprisonment (British Nationality Act 1948, Section 28 (1)). I, Frederick/Farrokh BULSARA of 22 Gladstone [Avenue], Feltham, [Middlesex] am of full age and capacity and was born at Zanaibar (Tanzania) on 5th September 1946 My father’s full name is Bomi Bulsara and he was born at Bulsar, [British] India on 14th December 1908 I am single (married) (a widower) (a widow) (divorced from my wife/husband) My (wife’s) (husband’s) full name (is) was…. And (she) (he) was born at … on… I am (a) a citizen of the following country or countries mentioned in section 1(3) of the British Nationality Act 1948, that is to say Zanzibar (Tanzania). (a) I am ordinarily resident in the United Kingdom (a) I have been ordinarily resident in the United Kingdom and colonies during the last five years as follows: 19 Hamilton Close, Feltham, [Middlesex] from 4-5-64 to 31-8-64 122 Hamilton Close, Feltham, [Middlesex] from 1-9-64 to 28-10-64 22 Gladstone [Avenue], Feltham, [Middlesex] from 29-10-64 to present day PTO Image 2 of 3 Freddie Mercury naturalisation certificate page two, 1969. Catalogue reference: HO 334/1421/117889 Transcript 8. The special circumstances in which I desire that the period of ordinary residence of Crown service shorter than five years which is mentioned in paragraph 7 above should be accepted are as follows:…. 9. I (have not) previously renounced or been deprived of citizenship of the United Kingdon and Colonies. [If the applicant has renounced citizenship of the United Kingdom and colonies, here state the date on which the declaration of renunciation was made; and if the applicant has been deprived of citizenship, state the date on which, and the authority by whom, the order of deprivation was made. 10. I hereby apply to be registered as a citizen of the United Kingdom and Colonies. [The application must be signed in the presence of one of the persons specified in the Appendix to the Instructions.] I, Frederick/Farrokh Bulsara so solemnly and sincerely declare that the foregoing particulars stated in this application are true and I make this solemn declaration conscientiously believing the same to be true. (Signature of applicant) F. Bulsara Made and subscribed this 21st Day of March 1969 Before me D S Mahany at Feltham (signed) D S Mahany [Here state whether Commissioner of Oaths, Justice of the Peace, Notary Public or other authorised person specified in the Appendix to the Instructions] A commissioner of oaths PLEASE DO NOT WRITE ANYTHING BELOW THIS LINE The above named applicant has been registered as a citizen of the United Kingdom and Colonies [signed] B Pinsent. 2 [June] 1969 Nationality Division, Home Office, London Image 3 of 3 Freddie Mercury in concert at Slane Castle, County Meath, Ireland, 1986. Copyright: Carol Lee / Alamy Why this record matters Date 2 June 1969 Catalogue reference HO 334/1421/117889 Freddie Mercury (1946–1991) is known to millions as the lead singer of the rock band Queen. He is widely celebrated for his powerful vocals and songwriting talent. Freddie was born Farrokh Bulsara in 1946 in Zanzibar, then a British Protectorate in the Indian Ocean just off the coast of East Africa. He and his family arrived in Feltham, West London in October 1964. Zanzibar had been a British Protectorate since 1890. It was a key centre of trade for spices, in particular cloves, nutmeg, pepper and cinnamon. Under the Zanzibar Act, passed by the UK government in December 1963, the territory was no longer part of the British Empire. Zanzibar became a constitutional monarchy (in which the monarch is head of state but the country is governed by elected officials) within the Commonwealth under the Sultan of Zanzibar. A month later, the Sultan was overthrown during the Zanzibar Revolution and a republic was established. In April 1964 the Republic of Zanzibar joined with Tanganyika, the mainland, and was known thereafter as Tanzania. Freddie and his family were among a number of British colonial staff and their families who left Zanzibar in the aftermath of the revolution. Settling in Feltham, Freddie enrolled in the graphic art and design course at the Ealing Technical College and School of Art (now part of the University of West London). In 1969 Freddie graduated college and became a British citizen by naturalisation. This is the legal process by which a person changes their nationality. To do this, he had to complete this form detailing personal information including his full name, birthplace, residence, and father's name. The form was then approved by the Home Office. The National Archives holds most of the surviving paperwork for successful naturalisations , up until 1986, including Freddie's. In the early 1970s, Freddie sang in bands in London. He became friends with Brian May and Roger Taylor, forming Queen in 1970. Freddie changed his name by deed poll at around this time. He appears to have opted not to enrol (make public record) this change of name with the High Court, so there is no permanent record of this in the public records. This is common, as enrolling a change of name by deed poll was more expensive and not a legal requirement. Queen broke through in Britain in 1974. Their popularity soared with the release of Bohemian Rhapsody in October 1975, which stayed at number one for nine weeks. By the early 1980s, Queen were drawing enormous crowds to their elaborately staged concerts. The band appeared at Live Aid in 1985 with Freddie’s spectacular performance going on to be a key cultural moment in musical history. The band continued to record and release music throughout the 1980s. On 23 November 1991 Freddie announced that he had been diagnosed with AIDS. He died from complications arising from his illness the following day. Freddie was 45 years old. Queen continued to release music after his death and his voice was still featuring in their work as late as 1995. In 2022, the US Library of Congress included Bohemian Rhapsody in the National Recording Registry. It is catalogued as: ‘an over the top musical thrill ride whose six minutes contained more technology-stretching bravado than most bands’ entire careers.’ View record details Discover highlights from the collection Explore the collection : Migration and citizenship Explore the collection : Postwar (1945–present) Help us improve this website Complete our short survey (opens in new tab) Back to top The National Archives Kew , Richmond TW9 4DU Follow us on social media X (formerly Twitter) YouTube Facebook Flickr Instagram Quick links About us Contact us News Blogs Podcasts Image library Press room Jobs British citizenship services Historical Manuscripts Commission Other websites UK Government Web Archive Legislation.gov.uk Find Case Law The Gazette The National Archives Trust Friends of The National Archives National Archives Design System Sign up to our emails Hear about our latest news, stories from the collection and priority booking for events. Menu Visit What’s on Explore the collection Help using the archive Education Professional guidance and services Search Shop Home Explore the collection Stories from the collection The story of James Stagg: The weatherman who turned the tide of D-Day The success of D-Day depended on the accurate forecasting of weather conditions by a team of meteorologists, led by James Stagg. Our records describe the pressure they were under and how they came to play a crucial role in the largest seaborn invasion in history. About this image The Allied leaders preparing their plans for the invasion of Europe. General Dwight D. Eisenhower is sat in the middle. Catalogue reference: INF 2/11 On this page Operation Overlord Stagg and his career Gathering the data Deciding when to launch Stormy weather D-Day Operation Overlord The D-Day landings, officially known as Operation Overlord, remain one of the most significant military operations in history. On 6 June 1944, Allied forces from several nations landed on the beaches of northern France. Here they opened a new front against Nazi Germany, which helped to bring about the end of the Second World War in Europe. While the scale of the operation was unprecedented, its success depended on more than military planning and manpower. Crucially, it relied on the accurate interpretation of weather conditions by a team of meteorologists led by Group Captain James Stagg. Their forecasts played a vital role in determining when the invasion could take place. Records at The National Archives, including reports and the weather forecasts they produced, detail their crucial work. Stagg and his career Born and educated in Scotland, Stagg earned his degrees from the University of Edinburgh before beginning his professional career as a science teacher. At the age of 24, he joined the British Meteorological Office (now the Met Office) as an assistant. During his time at the Meteorological Office, which was operated by the Air Ministry, the government department responsible for the Royal Air Force, he also served as a Senior Technical Officer. In 1932, he participated in a Royal Society polar expedition of Arctic Canada. Before the outbreak of the Second World War, he was appointed Superintendent of Kew Observatory – then the central observatory for the Meteorological Office. At the start of the Second World War, Stagg served as a civilian member of the meteorological service. In April 1944, he was granted an Emergency Commission as a Group Captain in the Royal Air Force Volunteer Reserve. He was subsequently appointed Chief Meteorological Officer at the Supreme Headquarters Allied Expeditionary Force (SHAEF) – the military command responsible for planning and executing the Allied invasion of northwest Europe. Here, Stagg led the team responsible for providing weather forecasts to senior Allied commanders including General Dwight D. Eisenhower who was the Supreme Allied Commander of SHAEF. Group Captain James Stagg, from the Imperial War Museum collection . Gathering the data Weather forecasting was considered a matter of national security during the Second World War, so much so that public weather forecasts were suspended for the duration of the conflict. This did not mean, however, that meteorological observations stopped. Accurate weather data remained essential for military planning, particularly in the lead-up to Operation Overlord. In an age before satellite technology, gathering this information was a challenging and complex task. In early 1944, a joint British-American Meteorological Section was established specifically to provide weather forecasts for D-Day. The team collected data from several sources. During the week before the planned invasion on 5 June, eight British and American weather ships were stationed at designated locations across the Atlantic to monitor and report atmospheric conditions. In addition, the Royal Air Force carried out a series of meteorological reconnaissance flights, although the information obtained from these missions was sometimes considered unreliable. Together with weather reports from the west coast of Ireland, these observations provided a broad picture of conditions across the North Atlantic. The data was then analysed by Stagg and his team who interpreted the forecasts. They then supplied senior SHAEF commanders with the information they needed to determine whether weather conditions were suitable for launching the invasion. Toggle transcript Chart of Weather in the Northern Hemisphere Morning of Monday 5th June 1944. GENERAL INFERENCE: A depression centred near the Shetlands is drifting northeast and beginning to ease up. There will be strong to gale force west to northwest winds in Shetland at first, moderating steadily. It will be mainly cloudy throughout the British Isles with showers in Scotland, N. England and N. Ireland and scattered showers further south at first; later showers are expected to die out in England, Ireland and S. Scotland. It will be rather cool in the South, cool in the North. FURTHER OUTLOOK: Rain spreading into W. Ireland, and W. Scotland later tomorrow afternoon moving east. Gale warning in operation in districts 13A, 13B. Time of issue 0800 4.6.44 and in districts 11,15, and 16 at 13.55 4.6.44. Weather forecast for the Northern Hemisphere on the morning of Monday 5 June 1944, the planned date for D-Day. Catalogue reference: AIR 37/1124A Deciding when to launch At the end of the war, a report was written examining the meteorological factors that influenced the choice of date for the Allied invasion. It concluded that the ideal conditions for the operation would have included light or calm winds and clear visibility unaffected by fog, mist, or haze. The report acknowledged, however, that such conditions were rarely achievable. As it noted: in English weather, even English summer weather, it was clearly impracticable to set up an ideal set of conditions and defer the assault until this set of conditions was obtained. Catalogue reference: CAB 106/976 In addition to military and political considerations, planners also had to account for the timing of high and low tides, as well as levels of natural illumination influenced by twilight and the phase and position of the moon. Consequently, the Allies agreed upon a set of minimum acceptable meteorological conditions under which the invasion could proceed. These criteria ultimately formed the basis for the decision to launch Operation Overlord on 6 June 1944. Even with agreed thresholds in place, however, the task of producing and interpreting weather forecasts was far from straightforward. The decision depended entirely on predictions of rapidly changing conditions, placing enormous pressure on those responsible for advising the Allied command. The intensity of these discussions is reflected in documents preserved at The National Archives. Toggle transcript The conference room was ANCXF Mess Room in Southwick House, a large room with a table at one end and easy chairs at the other; walls on three sides lined with bookcases, most of which were empty except for a certain number of books from the Navigation School at PORTSMOUTH which had been using the house for some time since their own headquarters was blitzed. The conference table was not used; the meetings were informal, those present using the easy chairs and the weather exposition being given at the very start. The weather situation was dealt with on each occasion by the Senior Meteorologist – Group Captain STAGG – who was accompanied by Commander PLEMING R.N. and Colonel YATES, U.S. Army Air Corps. Prior to this series the previous meetings to consider the weather had been held at SHAEF and on Monday, 29th May, 1944 Group Captain STAGG had given an optimistic long-range forecast with a considerable degree of confidence. However, on the Saturday night he had a different tale to tell. The long period of settled conditions was breaking up and the outlook for D-Day and the succeeding days was now most unpromising; in fact, the type of weather to be expected was such that made forecasting for more than 24 hours a very hazardous undertaking. D-Day weather report. Catalogue reference: AIR 37/1124A Stormy weather With the invasion initially scheduled for 5 June, a series of meetings began on the evening of Saturday 3 June to determine whether the operation should proceed as planned or be postponed. Forecasting conditions had been relatively uncomplicated up to that point, but by the weekend the weather had deteriorated significantly. Stagg later recalled that the changing conditions made reliable prediction much more difficult. As forecasts continued to be updated throughout the weekend, it became increasingly clear that the invasion could not go ahead on 5 June, as planned. Senior commanders met repeatedly to review the latest meteorological assessments and consider their implications. During a crucial meeting on the night of 4 June, Stagg and his team advised that a brief improvement in conditions was likely on 6 June. On the basis of this forecast, General Dwight D. Eisenhower made the decision to proceed, reportedly remarking: 'Well boys, there it is, I don't see how we can possibly do anything else.' Toggle transcript 2100, Sunday, 4th June. Supreme Commander’s meeting. Since the statement made before the meeting on Saturday evening, there have been some rapid and unexpected developments in the weather situation over the Atlantic. A front from one of the deep depressions in the northwest Atlantic has moved much farther south than was expected and is now traversing the Channel areas. It is almost over Portsmouth now and will clear the eastern Channel at least on the English side overnight. When that front has passed there will be an interval of fair conditions which, from the evidence we now have, should last until at least dawn on Tuesday. Wind speeds by Monday evening should decrease to Force 3-4 on the French Channel coasts and cloud will become mainly less than 5/10, with base 2-3000 ft. After that interval, lasting till Tuesday morning, cloud will probably increase to 8/10-10/10 from the west during Tuesday afternoon and will continue so overnight Tuesday. From a time on Wednesday which cannot be defined from present information, mainly cloudy conditions will continue; but there should be some intervals of broken cloud. In this period from Wednesday to Friday, there will probably be intervals of 10/10ths cloud with base at 1000 feet; these overcast intervals of low cloud may be expected to last 4-6 hours at a time. Report on the meteorological implications in the selection of the day for D-Day. Catalogue reference: CAB 106/976 Stagg later recorded the events in his diary. He recalled Eisenhower telling him: Well, Stagg, I promise you now that if this forecast of yours comes off, I'll give each of you a bottle of whiskey. General Dwight D. Eisenhower, Catalogue reference: CAB 106/976 D-Day In his entry for 6 June, Stagg wrote that he rose at 5am and reported to his post, where Admiral Creasy, Chief of Staff to Admiral Sir Bertram Ramsay, Commander of the Allied Naval Expeditionary Force, greeted him with the words: 'You must feel a tremendous load off your shoulders, Stagg. Anyway, you can feel proud of your forecast.' Soon afterwards, the invasion began. The forecasts had been made, the decision had been taken, and the success of the operation would now depend on events unfolding across the English Channel. In the early hours of 6 June 1944, more than 150,000 Allied troops landed by sea and air onto five beaches in Normandy, France. While the weather conditions were not perfect, it was better than the previous day – Stagg's judgement had proved correct. The Allied troops were able to make good progress, despite heavy casualties. By the end of the day, they had taken all the beaches they had set out to hold. Eisenhower, who went on to become the 34th president of the United States, would later commend James Stagg's team, writing: I wish you to express my appreciation to the members of your section and the meteorological personnel of subordinate and associated agencies whose combined goodwill and co-operation contributed so much to the final results. General Dwight D. Eisenhower, Catalogue reference: AIR 73/8 Toggle transcript SECRET SUPREME HEADQUARTERS ALLIED EXPEDITIONARY FORCE Office of the Supreme Commander 28 June 1944 SUBJECT: Commendation TO: Group Captain J.M. Stagg, OBE, Chief, Meteorological Section, G-3 Division, SHAEF. I desire to commend you for the skilful operation of the meteorological services in support of the ‘OVERLORD’ assault on the Continent of EUROPE. I wish you to express my appreciation to the members of your section and the meteorological personnel of subordinate and associated agencies whose combined goodwill and co-operation contributed so much to the final results. Through the months preceding D day your tireless efforts, good judgement, skill and sound leadership resulted in the development of a procedure capable of utilizing the talents and facilities of both nations and all services in a unified manner. I have been particularly impressed with the sound approach made by you to the difficult task of coordinating all agencies. I have noted with assurance your deep sense of responsibility and integrity in presenting all facts precisely as they were conceived to be. Your straight-forward attitude in presenting the weather situations and forecasts, frequently under the most difficult conditions, permitted me to reach decisions with confidence that I was acting on the best information and advice obtainable. This service on your part, and on the part of those associated with you, merits very special commendation as an outstanding contribution to the success of the whole operation. (Signed) Dwight D. Eisenhower DWIGHT D. EISENHOWER General, U.S. Army Letter from Dwight Eisenhower to James Stagg. Catalogue reference: AIR 73/8 After the war Stagg returned to the Met Office. In 1971 he published Forecast for Overlord, in which he gave his account of D-Day. He died on 23 June 1975 at the age of 74. Menu Visit What’s on Explore the collection Help using the archive Education Professional guidance and services Search Shop Home Explore the collection Stories from the collection Focus on IVF and reproductive technology in the archive About this image A close up of a diagram explaining the fertilisation process. Catalogue reference: FD 7/2308 During its development, many considered in vitro fertilisation (IVF) unethical. Records at The National Archives highlight how this view has changed over time and brings to light the people who fought for, and against, its use. Author Dr Laura Robson-Mainwaring Roles Author Researcher Principal Records Specialist – Modern Health On this page Louise Brown: A glimmer of hope Filming the first IVF birth Developing IVF A new technology raises new questions Voices from the public: Fear and hope A new world The legacy of IVF Louise Brown: A glimmer of hope In July 1978, the world witnessed a medical milestone: the birth of Louise Brown, the first baby conceived through in vitro fertilisation (IVF). The technique, developed by Patrick Steptoe, Robert Edwards, and Jean Purdy, involves fertilising an egg outside the body before transferring the embryo to the uterus. The success of this process marked the beginning of a scientific and social transformation. In the late 1960s and early 1970s, well before Louise’s birth, the press began sharing concerns about IVF. UK Government records, held by The National Archives, show that this publicity alarmed the public and many people were concerned about the ethical implications of IVF. For couples experiencing infertility, however, these medical developments created hope and presented a potential path to parenthood. Image 1 of 2 Newspaper clipping from The Guardian for an article titled 'Time ripe for first tube baby', 4 January 1972. Catalogue reference: MH 166/928 Image 2 of 2 Newspaper clipping from the Daily Sketch for an article titled 'Doctor in plea for test tube baby inquiry', 2 November 1970. Catalogue reference: MH 166/928 Previous Next Image 1 of 2 Image 2 of 2 From our collection MH 166/928 Title Government consultation, correspondence and minutes of meetings regarding IVF Date 1965–1973 At this time, advances in reproductive medicine, IVF, surrogacy, and later gene editing, created profound ethical questions such as: When does human life begin? Is it acceptable to manipulate embryos? Who holds parental rights? How should society guard against exploitation and unequal access? Today, IVF is a well-accepted part of reproductive healthcare. In 2023 alone, one in every 32 births in the UK were the result of IVF treatment, which is equivalent to one child in every classroom. In the late 1970s and early 1980s, however, the technology was unprecedented and considered controversial. Filming the first IVF birth A file (catalogue reference: INF 12/13/1399) from the Central Office of Information (COI) shows the widespread public interest surrounding Louise Brown’s birth. Ministers decided to commission the COI to produce an official film. This footage would assess the baby’s condition at birth and create a historical record of IVF’s use. Lesley Brown (Louise’s mother) also decided to sell her story exclusively to Associated Newspapers Ltd (Daily Mail) before entering Oldham General District Hospital. This meant, frustratingly for the Department of Health and Social Security (DHSS), that there would be a 28–day embargo (waiting period) before any footage they recorded could be shared publicly. On Monday 24 July, the DHSS asked the COI’s Films Division to be ready to film the birth of the world’s first IVF baby. Our records show that, throughout the day, COI stayed in touch with the Regional Health Authority and Steptoe, who confirmed that the birth would not happen before Thursday evening. On that basis, the film crew was told to stand down for 24 hours, but everything changed the next morning. At 11:30 am on Tuesday 25 July, Tony Buckingham from the Regional Health Authority phoned with an urgent warning that the birth could happen at any moment. As a result, the COI sent the film crew racing to Oldham. Final filming rights were secured, including from Mrs Brown at 11:15 pm. Just 15 minutes later at 11:30 pm, the caesarean section began. Louise was born at 11:47 pm, weighing 5 lbs 12 oz. The footage is preserved at the British Film Institute (BFI) and made available online by Wellcome Collection. Toggle transcript TEST TUBE BABY 24 MINUTE NEWS ITEM At 23.47 BST on 25 July 1978 a unique baby was born in Britain - the result of a "test-tube" fertilisation. Louise Joy Brown, the 51b 12oz daughter of Mr and Mrs Brown of Bristol, was delivered safely by Caesarian section by Patrick Steptoe Esq FRCS FRCOG, Honarary Consultant Gynaecologist at the Oldham General Hospital near Manchester. He was assisted by Dr John Webster MB ChB MRCOG, by Dr Finlay Campbell FSARCS DA (Anaesthetist), Theatre Sister Astel SRN and Sister Marshall SRN, Dr. Hilson MAMB BChir FRCP(L) FRCP(E) MRCS DCH (Consultant Paediatrician). Also present at the birth was Dr Robert Edwards DSc PhD, the Cambridge physiologist whose 20 years of research led to the successful fertilisation. The historic birth was commented on by Dr Edwards as "A close collaboration between scientist and doctor". Length: 86 1/2 ft 26.33 metres Time: 2 mins 24 secs at 24 fps 2 mins 17 secs at 25 fps Sales enquiries please to: Sales Unit Film and Television Division Central Office of Information Hercules Road London SEl Tel. 01-928 2345, Ext 227 or 224 Telex 91544 CENTROFORM LDN Memorandum showing the description of the two minute news reel produced by the COI at the birth of Louise Brown, 1978. There was a longer (15 minute) clinical version , narrated by Steptoe. Please note, both videos contain graphic depictions of a medical procedure (a cesarean section). Catalogue reference: INF 12/1399 From our collection INF 12/1399 Title Central Office of Information's notes on their film coverage of the birth of the first 'test tube' baby Date July–October 1978 Developing IVF In the early 1970s, Edwards and Steptoe were developing techniques that would eventually lead to Louise’s birth. Records of the Medical Research Council (MRC) show that they applied for funding in May 1971 but were turned down on ethical grounds. For most of the 1970s, the MRC viewed IVF as too experimental, too risky, and too poorly supported by clinical infrastructure to justify funding . The MRC instead encouraged them to undertake studies on animals. Toggle transcript 2. Long-term support declined (a) Dr R.G. Edwards (University of Cambridge) and Mr P.C. Steptoe (consultant gynaecologist, Oldham): application for long-term support for studies on human reproduction (MRC 71/239). The application was declined because of serious doubts about the ethical aspects of the proposed investigations, especially those relating to the implantation in women of oocytes fertilized in vitro which were considered premature. Dr Edwards should, however, be encouraged, without commitment, to undertake studies of the type proposed in animals. Medical Research Council Meeting ‘Long-term support denied’, 20 May 1971, Catalogue reference: FD 13/171 From our collection FD 13/171 Title Notes from the Medical Research Council's Meeting Date May 1971 Despite the rejection, their research continued with private funding. After the safe and successful birth of the first IVF baby, Louise, the MRC became a strong supporter of IVF research. This opened the door to mainstream clinical development and a state-focused examination of the ethical issues involved. A new technology raises new questions The Committee of Inquiry into Human Fertilisation and Embryology, chaired by the moral philosopher Dame Mary Warnock, was established in 1982 by the DHSS. Its members included doctors, scientists, a psychologist, and faith representatives, reflecting the scientific, social, and moral issues at stake. Together, they discussed whether IVF should be permitted, and if so, how it should be regulated. They also discussed the moral status of an embryo created in a laboratory and whether the state should regulate who could access IVF. The fundamental moral objection to IVF was that, for the procedure to be successful, several eggs must be fertilised, meaning that some embryos are likely to be destroyed or discarded during the process. This is because not all embryos develop successfully, so multiple embryos are created to increase the chances of a successful pregnancy. Despite this, their final report approved the use of IVF, with some limitations, and recommended the creation of a voluntary licensing authority, an independent body that would monitor IVF clinics to ensure ethical standards were being followed. It also concluded that commercial surrogacy was unethical, meaning the carrier of an embryo cannot be paid by the parent(s) for carrying their baby. Additionally, the committee suggested that human embryos used in research should not be kept alive in vitro beyond 14 days as this would be unethical. Although the report was signed by all members, differing views on when life begins led to expressions of dissent within the report that, they claimed, ‘ reflected the range of views in society ’. The report went on to lay the basis for the regulatory framework established by the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act 1990. Toggle transcript MRC/RCOG Voluntary Licensing Authority for Human In Vitro Fertilisation and Embryology. Guidelines for both clinical and research applications of Human In Vitro Fertilisation 1985. The Voluntary Licensing Authority (VLA) is jointly sponsored by the Medical Research Council and the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists. Guidelines for clinical and research applications for Human In Vitro Fertilisation from the voluntary licensing authority,1985. Catalogue reference: FD 7/3321 From our collection FD 7/3321 Title Reports, notes and correspondence on IVF Date 1986–1989 Voices from the public: Fear and hope Letters from ordinary people, found in the archive, capture the emotional and moral intensity of the public debate around IVF. One correspondent wrote, 'Research babies in bottles’, I’ve never heard of anything so repulsive. Letter from a member of the public to the Secretary of State for Social Services, 2 November 1970., Catalogue reference: MH 166/928 We heartily disapprove of this research, because if nature decides that children should not be born then artificial means should not be used. Imagine a child having to realise he was a test tube child. Letter from a member of the public to the Lord President of the Council, 30 January 1974., Catalogue reference: INF 12/1399 Toggle transcript February 26th 1967. The Minister of Health Dear Sir In view of the clear admission on ITN news this evening that experiments on human foetuses will be a necessary preliminary to the successful implantation in the womb of eggs fertilised outside the human body, would you kindly give me an answer to the following points: a) do yon personally approve of this technique in making childbirth possible? b) Do you personally consider that there are no ethical objections to the experimentation currently in progress? c) Are National Health and/or University facilities being used for this research? d) Have you power to direct that such experiments cease? e) If so, will you provide the direction the medical profession is seeking, and order an immediate cessation of these activities? You can no doubt deduce my own attitude. Yours sincerely John Wilson (Liberal Prospective Parliamentary Candidate for Hemel Hempstead) Letter from Parliamentary Candidate John Wilson to the Minister of Health, 26 February 1967. Catalogue reference: MH 166/928 Others wrote pleading for access to treatment, revealing the emotional toll of infertility and the personal stakes behind the debates. One couple who had been married for ten years described themselves as living ‘in a hopeless condition’ and asked to ‘participate in this service to humanity… We are willing to accept your terms of payment (whatever it may be).’ Toggle transcript 12th May ‘73 The Ministry of Health, London Re: Test Tube Babies Sir Recently in one of our local papers we came across one article which has inspired us to write this letter. We are a sterile couple, married for the last ten years: in the 7th year of our married life my Mrs had to undergo an emergency operation. Right phallopean [sic] tube bursted [sic] due to advanced ectopic pregnancy (approx. 2 ½ months). While cutting and clamping the doctors thought it wise to remove cyst from left tube also, however unfortunately the second tube along with cyst was removed, leaving us completely incapable to conceive & in hopeless condition. We accepted the life as if we have lost a limb & are living the life of satisfaction. However when we read the report in the paper that in U.K. you are successful in planting fertilised ovum in the womb and baby could develop thereafter. We have thought it wise to refer this matter to you and we wonder whether we could participate in this service to humanity & be benefited with your success. We are willing to accept your terms of payment etc (whatever it may be). It will be in order to mention here that we are a couple of 35/33 yrs of age (husb/wife) physically fit. Sperm count: 120 million/cc & all other qualities/quantities being above normal: m.c. regular. If you require any certificate or any medical opinion/ questioning to be answered we will be too glad to furnish the same. We hope you will extend you helping hand before we get too old to participate. Sincerely thanking you [signature]. A letter from a couple dealing with fertility challenges to the Ministry of Health, 12 May 1973. Catalogue reference: MH 156/458 Patients of Patrick Steptoe also wrote in his defence. After spotting a local newspaper report in Oldham’s Evening Chronicle suggesting his work was a step toward euthanasia, one woman passionately directed her letter to Prime Minister James Callaghan: Mr Steptoe is my doctor, and I am involved in these ‘experiments’ as they put it…. I have met so many young women in Dr Kershaws Hospital whilst we have been receiving treatment, we all love Mr Steptoe very much indeed, he is our only hope to have a child of our own, he is a kind, considerate and very wonderful man, and all he is trying to do is help us, we have no other hope, at all… It’s a terrible thing to be told you can’t have a child, and then all of a sudden you meet Mr Steptoe and there’s a glimmer of hope. A patient of Dr Steptoe to the Prime Minister James Callaghan, undated letter., Catalogue reference MH 156/458 Toggle transcript …that a Mr. A Mcgarty was going to ask you to investigate Mr Steptoe’s work, this is why I’m writing to you put ‘our’ side of the story to you as well. I say ‘our’ because I have met so many young women in the Kershaw’s Hospital whilst we have been receiving treatment, we all love Mr Steptoe very much indeed, he is our only hope to have a child of our own, he is a kind, considerate man, and all he is trying to do is help us, we have no other hope, at all. Please, ask your wife her feelings, as a women, I’m sure she’ll understand, it’s a terrible thing to be told you can’t have… Page from multi-page letter from a patient of Dr Steptoe to the Prime Minister James Callaghan, undated letter. Catalogue reference MH 156/458 From our collection MH 156/458 Title Background documents and correspondence on IVF and the birth of Louise Brown Date 1973–1979 Another patient of Steptoe, describing the treatment as her only hope, wrote: If the people objecting to this treatment had experiences the torment and misery of a woman who is unable to conceive I am sure they would look at this matter in a different light. Letter from a patient of Dr Steptoe to her local MP, 22 May 1969., Catalogue reference: FD 9/1430 From our collection FD 9/1430 Title Enquiries from the public on IVF research Date 1969–1973 A new world Following the successful birth of Louise Brown, Steptoe, Edwards and Purdy worked towards founding Bourn Hall, which became the world’s first IVF clinic in 1980. Here, they worked to advance IVF techniques. Around this time, advancements were also happening across the globe, with the world’s second IVF baby being born in October 1978 in Kolkata, India. Image 1 of 2 Extracts of a leaflet for Bourn Hall IVF Clinic, 1985. Catalogue reference: FD 7/3334 Image 2 of 2 The leaflet reads, 'Collecting these samples will be organised by the nursing staff. The results of the hormone investigations will enable the time of ovulation to be accurately predicted. (b) When ovulation is imminent, the wife will be notified that the egg recovery procedure will shortly take place, and she will be prepared for the operation, which is again a laparoscopy technique. Based on the Clinic's work to date, the percentage of eggs recovered is very high. (c) When the time of ovulation is diagnosed, the husband will be asked to attend the Clinic to provide a fresh semen sample, for fertilisation of his wife's egg. The process of fertilisation is carried out in an exceptionally sterile environment and the embryology work of nurturing the embryo to the stage where replacement can be effected takes approximately 3 days. The percentage of eggs successfully fertilised is over 80%. (d) Replacement of the fertilised egg (embryo) will be carried out in the operating theatre, usually without anaesthesia. (e) A period of a few hours rest and medical care will then follow, until the wife is advised she can leave. ... Previous Next Image 1 of 2 Image 2 of 2 From our collection FD 7/2308 Title Files from the inquiry into Human Fertilisation and Embryology (Warnock Committee). Date 1982–1984 From our collection FD 7/3334 Title Files related to Bourn Hall Clinic, Cambridge. Date 1985–1989 Sadly, Jean Purdy passed away in 1985 after helping to develop and refine the laboratory techniques that made IVF possible. Patrick Steptoe died in 1988, having helped transform fertility treatment through his pioneering work in laparoscopy and IVF alongside Edwards. Their contributions established IVF as a viable medical option for overcoming infertility and offered hope to millions of couples worldwide. Following Steptoe's death, Dame Mary Donaldson, Chair of the Voluntary Licensing Authority, described him as: ... a man of pioneering spirit but also one of great integrity. His death marks the end of an era but his influence will undoubtedly spread into the next. Dame Mary Donaldson to Mrs P Steptoe, 23 March 1988, Catalogue reference: FD 7/3334 Bourn Hall Clinic still operates today, and Steptoe, Edwards, and Purdy’s work continues to have a global impact. The legacy of IVF The archival material surrounding the development of IVF is invaluable for understanding how governments and society responded to the challenges posed by new reproductive technologies. While IVF is not a definitive cure for infertility and does not always succeed, it continues to offer hope to many. This was made possible by the pioneering work of figures such as Steptoe, Edwards, and Purdy, as well as the persistent hope of the hundreds of women involved in their early experiments. nhs.uk Would you like to learn more about IVF? results.title: Home front India: Women’s experiences in a Second World War battle zone

Menu Visit What’s on Explore the collection Help using the archive Education Professional guidance and services Search Shop Home Explore the collection Stories from the collection Focus on Home front India: Women’s experiences in a Second World War battle zone About this image Manipuri women who appear to be waiting at an airfield to begin work in loading or unloading’. Catalogue reference: AIR 23/1956 A small set of photographs in our collection shows women from Manipur, India at work on an airfield during the Second World War. What was their experience of living on the ‘home front’ at the heart of one of the most brutal battles of the conflict? Author Dr Elizabeth Haines Roles Author Researcher Principal Records Specialist – Empire and Commonwealth On this page Women in a battle zone Experiences of the conflict The war in context Ambiguous legacies Important information ! This article includes references to armed violence, starvation, homelessness and sexual violence. An image of a document contains an ethnic slur. These are included here to accurately represent historical records and people’s past experiences. Women in a battle zone A small number of photographs of the 1944 Siege of Imphal – the capital city of the state of Manipur, North Eastern India – can be found in the records of the Royal Air Force (RAF). A report of around 60 pages, held by The National Archives as AIR 23/1956, focuses on military logistics but also describes the living conditions of those posted there. From our collection AIR 23/1956 Title Narrative on the Siege of Imphal, India, March to June 1944 Date 1945 Members of the British Army, the Indian Army, the RAF and the United States Air Force all found themselves in the city during one of the key battles of the Second World War. The Battle of Imphal was polled (jointly with the nearby battle of Kohima) as 'Britain’s Greatest Battle' by a poll from the National Army Museum in 2013. In the course of the Second World War, the valley had received thousands of exhausted civilian refugees retreating from Burma (present day Myanmar) in early 1942, and had been bombed since December 1942 by the Japanese military. The wider state of Manipur had been partially invaded by the Japanese and subjected to a scorched earth policy by the Allies – the systematic destruction of resources that could later benefit the enemy. In some parts every single building was destroyed. As a frontline of the war, the rice-growing valley became a military camp. North Eastern India received 340,000 Indian troops, 100,000 British troops, 90,000 African troops, 65,000 Chinese troops and 10,000 American troops. The Imphal valley alone at one point held 200,000 troops for 330,000 inhabitants. Over half of the houses owned by Meitei (the Tibeto-Burman people who make up the larger part of the population in the valley) were requisitioned for military purposes. New road infrastructures changed the landscape entirely, and food supplies and labour patterns were transformed. This map printed by the Allied Land Forces South East Asia in 1944 show the movement of the 15th Division of the Japanese Army (in blue) towards and into the Imphal valley between March and June. Catalogue reference: WO 252/1444 The photographs show an airfield where women are working and talking, alongside the soldiers, planes and military technologies supporting an unprecedented jungle warfare campaign. Framed by an unknown photographer, these may be some of a very small number of images that show Manipuri women at work during the conflict. Toggle transcript Manipuris show a keen interest in long range petrol tanks. Photograph of Manipuri women possibly being shown to lift aircraft petrol tanks. They appear very young, and their clothing and hair suggest that some may be fairly recent brides. Catalogue reference: AIR 23/1956 While the impact of the Second World War on many places around the world has barely been recorded, the longer history of Imphal and Manipur has been politically contested and more closely studied. Historians have used both written sources and oral history accounts to bring better understanding of what that moment meant. In the military report in AIR 23/1956, and in the original captions for the photographs, the women are framed as exotic, attractive and useful to the war effort. Wider sources, however, invite us to consider the experience of the war from women’s own points of view. Experiences of the conflict Japan Lan (Japan War), as it is known in Meitei, was a moment of incredibly rapid change for individuals and society in Manipur. In first-hand accounts and in oral histories that have been collected we can see the ambiguities and contradictions, opportunity and desolation that characterised the experience of living in a battle zone. Many of those in this article come from How Women Remember War, a compilation of oral histories published in 2019 by Leisangthem Gitarani Devi . Witness accounts demonstrate that the war brought violence and fear. The report in AIR 23/1956 mentions that bombing in 1944 killed ‘a certain number of civilian Manipuris’. Wider reports by the colonial administration and oral histories show that bombing by the Japanese destroyed entire residential areas and marketplaces. The only shelters from this threat were trenches with branches and leaves. The plane began bombing the trench … my sister and elder brother were deeper inside. They were buried in the mud. The following morning, they had to be dug out with hands. Yumkhaibam ongbi Manjuri Apart from the danger of being killed by bullets or shells there was also the danger of being bitten by snakes in the trenches. Thokchom Ramani The town of Imphal as seen from the sky in December 1943. This image is part of a series documenting the frontier between British India and Burma, particularly roads, rivers, airfields and other lines of communication. Catalogue reference: CN 1/7 Forests and agricultural land were both requisitioned and destroyed by armed forces on both sides, and food was diverted to the troops. We didn’t have any food. We would often fill our stomachs with water chestnut [from a large lake] when there was no rice available for days … They [the soldiers] burnt all the houses and the granaries. We lost a lot of food grains. We were asked to evacuate our houses. We fled the war for about a year. Pukhrambam Ningol Khwairakpam ongbi Madhumati Several accounts describe how the presence of large numbers of male troops was a threat to women. They [the Allied soldiers] treated children very affectionately. However, at night, they would come asking for women. Women couldn’t venture out at night. Groups of men kept vigil at night with sticks and swords. Thokchom Ramani In the face of all of this, the accounts show that the encounter with military technology was still enthralling. They [aeroplanes] used to fly very, very high like swallows. They would emit smoke in the sky all around, and we would especially watch the trails of smoke. Madhumati For an orphaned Manipuri boy, who later wrote an autobiography, The Second World War in Manipur And My Childhood, it was captivating: Every day and night, thousands of different vehicles, quite strange to this place were ceaselessly coming in, carrying soldiers, guns, technicians... We hardly remembered our personal sorrows in the midst of all that grandeur of war. Khuraijam Nimaicharan Singh In Meitei society in the early 20th century women were important contributors to household income. One major market in Imphal was exclusively run by women vendors. However, the war also shifted the kinds of work that women were likely to be doing. AIR 23/1956 describes women as loading and unloading transport aircraft that were bringing troops and supplies ‘a work in which the cheerful and gaily-clad Manipuri women would laughingly collaborate’. Most accounts agree that labouring work for the Allied armed forces was well-paid, although some women reported being ashamed of taking on this kind of manual labour. Toggle transcript Dakota aircraft carried a wide variety of equipment to the Imphal Valley. Since all land communications had been cut by the Japanese, no M.T. could reach the garrison, and small vehicles such as jeeps were flown in by transport aircraft. This photograph gives a sense of the airfield as the meeting of military and civilian, with men in uniform loading the plane and women in civilian clothes working in parallel. Catalogue reference: AIR 23/1956 However, women were also involved in heavier labour such as the construction of the the vital all-weather airfield at Imphal. Once the tractor had laid the road, women carried all the stones and mud and many other things for tarring the road. Khuraijam Nimaicharan Singh Koirengei As property was destroyed and their livelihoods disrupted more women took up sex work. [During the war] women couldn’t go out for over two months. They had to stop their businesses in the market. So they started trading their flesh for money… these women would often come back and take care of their children. Yumkhaibam Manjuri The war in context Even these brief extracts describing the effect of the war suggest how Manipuri sources offer a more ambiguous picture of the Allies than we often encounter in the UK. Situating the years 1942 to 1944 in the longer history of the Imphal Valley give a better context to this moment of extreme conflict within the lives of the valley's inhabitants. Manipur was only formally integrated into the British Empire as part of British India less than 50 years before the outbreak of the Second World War. At earlier moments Imphal had been part of the Toungoo Empire, centred around today’s Myanmar. By the time of the Japanese invasion in 1942, Manipuri women had succeeded in turning back British colonial policy twice, in events known in Meitei as Nupi Lan (women’s wars). In 1904 women had successfully protested forced labour that had been imposed as a form of collective punishment. In 1939, at the outbreak of the war, thousands of women had conducted a market boycott to resist the export of rice that was causing famine conditions in Manipur. After several days of protest and enduring armed violence, they succeeded in this too. While these photographs show the women working for the Allied forces, it might be wrong to interpret that they supported the Allies' cause. Toggle transcript In dry weather the difficulties of rain and mud are replaced by the dust hazard. At Kangla, a fair-weather strip near Imphal, hundreds of transport aircraft landed daily, and at times the dust raised an impenetrable fog. The photo gives a good impression of conditions. In the foreground, are Manipuri women who are employed by the Air Forces and by the Army. Manipuri women who appear to be waiting at an airfield to begin work in loading or unloading, standing close to aeroplanes described elsewhere as like ‘swallows’. Catalogue reference: AIR 23/1956 Some Indians in the 1940s saw co-operation with the Japanese as a faster route to self-governance than loyalty to the British. Historians have shown that some Manipuris joined the Indian National Army, and fought on the side of the Japanese at Imphal. Intense propaganda campaigns were made by both sides. Records from the British administration and Japanese forces show that they were both keen to keep the people at the centre of the destruction in the Imphal Valley on ‘their side’. Commit no offences whatever against them… The Indians have for years been awaiting their delivery at our hands. The Commander of the Japanese forces to his troops at Imphal. Catalogue reference: CAB 106/50 A letter from the representative of the British Indian government in Manipur describes the destruction of Manipuri communities taking place in Imphal in 1944: If many more of them see their houses, property and food destroyed by us, they can hardly be expected to remain enthusiastically pro-British. E. F. Lydall, Political Agent in Manipur, 16 April 1944. Catalogue reference: WO 203/3200 He describes the effect of the Allied ‘Scorched Earth’ policy on the Imphal valley and asks for more attention from the military to the living conditions of the communities that have been displaced. Toggle partial transcript Economically, the piling up of villagers in increasing crowded conditions presents an immediate problem and the destruction of paddy and the prospect of considerable areas of paddy land being cultivated inadequately or not at all is one which forces one to envisage famine conditions in the devastated and evacuated areas. These so far are approximately all areas near the foothills to the north, north-east, south-east and south of the valley, as well as the area south of Bishenpur. Politically, the Manipuris have already had their confidence severely shaken by the Japanese invasion of their country, great play having been made in the last few years that they must not mind giving up their houses to the military who were here to defend them from the enemy. If many more of them see their houses, property and food destroyed by us, they can hardly be expected to remain enthusiastically pro-British. Letter from E. F. Lydall, the Political Agent (representative of the British Indian government) in Manipur, 16 April 1944. Catalogue reference: WO 203/3200 The tensions of being at the site of conflict between empires are reflected in oral history. Some accounts from men and women speak favourably of their relationships with the Japanese invaders. Ambiguous legacies The extent of the destruction caused by both Allies and Japanese mean that for many Manipuris, the surrender of the Japanese forces did not mean a ‘win’. The end of the war left the Imphal valley entirely transformed. Record revealed Japanese Instrument of Surrender, 1945 After six years of brutal global conflict, this document marked the end of the Second World War. Some eventually received compensation to rebuild with, first from the Manipur government, and later from the independent Indian government. Other changes were permanent. Still a borderland territory, the new infrastructure meant that post-war Imphal was far less rural. It was now at the centre of a road network connecting India and Burma. The strengthening of the British presence and social change had meant a weakening of the Manipuri royalty. In 1947 Manipur became the first princely state in Asia to have democratic government. Separatist movements remain active in Manipur, which has been governed under a state of emergency since it was declared a ‘disturbed territory’ by the Indian government in 1958. The fairly rapid retreat of the Allies left weapons behind, and the roads network into northwest Burma became and remains an important route for drug-smuggling. For most of the 80 years since the Second World War, women have continued to survive alongside armed conflict, most recently insurgents and counter-insurgency forces. Some of the Manipuri women whose oral histories of the Second World War have been recorded were among the Meira Paibi movement (women bearing flaming torches). They have been campaigning for citizens’ rights, particularly protection for women against violence, through night-patrols and protests since the 1970s. The images in AIR 23/1956, far more than the words in the report, open up reflection on how ‘Britain’s Greatest Battle’ was lived on the front-line by the women who found themselves caught up in that short moment, and in its legacy. They point to the ongoing work that is needed to build a fuller understanding of the impact of the Second World War in India, and of the complex legacies it has had in South Asia and beyond. Further reading Leishangthem Gitarani Devi (2019), How Women Remember War: Unearthing Memories of the Second World War in Manipur , Zubaan Publishers Pvt.
